No experiments have been run, so there is no evidence yet about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion matters. 2. config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA with 2000 components) is the simplest configuration in the space. It sets a reference baseline, so later experiments can each change one factor and be compared against it: RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT), modality (image-only, multimodal), or profile setting and aggregation (multiprofile with avgpool or transformer). 3. Under a limited budget, an interpretable baseline is the most useful first experiment. It lets us measure whether added complexity actually improves accuracy, rather than assuming it does, and it avoids starting with a configuration that changes many design choices at once.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: The only result so far is the RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (accuracy 0.485, F1 0.464). We have no information on whether the imaging modality carries useful signal, and most of the remaining search space (36 of 50 configurations) is multimodal. 2. What this tests: The image-only, single-profile ResNet50 configuration keeps the profile setting fixed and uses no aggregation or fusion. This gives a clean unimodal image baseline to compare directly against the RNA baseline. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: Whether images are weaker than, comparable to, or stronger than RNA largely decides how much of the remaining budget should go to multimodal fusion versus RNA encoder and profile-setting variants. Running this before any multimodal or multiprofile experiment avoids changing several design choices at once and makes later multimodal results interpretable.

1. Evidence so far: RNA-only with PCA (config_001, acc 0.485, F1 0.464) clearly beats image-only with ResNet50 (config_010, acc 0.208, F1 0.172). RNA looks like the stronger modality. However, we have only these two runs, and the profile setting is still completely unexplored. 2. What this tests: config_002 keeps the best-known setup (RNA-only, PCA) and changes one thing, switching from single-profile to multi-profile with the simplest aggregation (avgpool). This isolates whether pooling several profiles helps. 3. Why it is the best next run: profile setting is a structural choice that affects about two-thirds of the remaining search space, so its answer guides most later decisions. Starting from the strong RNA baseline gives a clean, high-signal comparison. Avgpool is the cheapest, lowest-variance test, and comparisons of transformer aggregation, other encoders, or multimodal fusion can follow.

1. Evidence: RNA is clearly the stronger modality so far (0.485 vs 0.208 accuracy for image-only). Moving the PCA RNA model from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool gave a large gain (0.485 to 0.591 accuracy; F1 0.464 to 0.573). Multiprofile is therefore the most promising direction. We do not yet know whether the aggregation method matters. 2. This experiment keeps the best configuration fixed (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000) and changes only avgpool to transformer. That isolates the effect of aggregation and shows whether a learned, attention-based summary across profiles adds value beyond simple averaging. 3. It builds directly on the strongest result with a single-variable change, so it tests a likely improvement while also answering a design question. The answer shapes many later choices, because aggregation appears in most of the remaining multiprofile and multimodal configurations. Testing multimodal fusion or other RNA encoders before settling this would leave a key, widely shared factor unresolved.

Test: config_037 is identical to config_025 except that the RNA encoder is scVI instead of PCA. It is also config_005 with ViT-L image features added through weighted fusion. Why now: It exploits the best-supported settings for representation, profile setting, aggregation and fusion while changing only one factor relative to two existing runs. Either outcome is informative and directly guides the remaining budget, and it is the most likely candidate for a new best.

Either outcome reduces uncertainty on the design choice with the least evidence, and it does so more efficiently than re-testing fusion or encoders, which already have clearer support.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only scVI with multiprofile avgpool (config_005, accuracy 0.650, F1 0.628). Measuring its effect first on the strong RNA modality tells us whether later budget should go to multiprofile variants (aggregation, fusion) or to single-profile encoder and fusion comparisons. The result is informative whichever way it comes out.

1. Evidence: RNA is the strong modality (0.485 accuracy, versus 0.208 for ResNet50 image-only). Moving PCA RNA from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool gave a large gain (0.591 accuracy, 0.573 F1), so multiprofile RNA is the most promising direction so far. The aggregation method remains untested, and it is a key design choice for every multiprofile configuration, including the multimodal ones. 2. Test: config_003 keeps everything from the current best (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000) and changes only avgpool to transformer. This isolates whether learned attention over profiles beats simple mean pooling. 3. Value: it exploits the strongest result so far while answering a clean single-variable question. The answer will guide aggregation choices across the many remaining multiprofile configurations. RNA encoder choice (scVI, scGPT) is a natural follow-up once the aggregation choice is clearer.

1) Evidence so far: RNA is far stronger than image (0.485 for RNA single-profile vs 0.208 for ResNet50 single-profile). Multiprofile avgpool clearly beats single-profile for PCA RNA (0.591 vs 0.485, with F1 agreeing). Transformer aggregation underperformed avgpool (0.519). The best setting so far is RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool, but only one RNA representation (pca_n2000) has been tested, so the effect of the RNA encoder is still unknown. 2) This experiment keeps the best setting fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and swaps only the encoder from PCA to scGPT. Any change in performance can then be attributed to the representation alone. 3) RNA is the dominant modality, so the RNA encoder choice will likely carry into every later multimodal configuration. Testing a pretrained foundation-model encoder in the best-known setting both exploits the strongest direction and resolves a major open design question. That makes it more efficient than adding a weak image modality before the RNA backbone is settled.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only PCA multiprofile with avgpool (config_002, acc 0.591, F1 0.573). Multiprofile avgpool clearly beat singleprofile (0.485) and transformer aggregation (0.519). PCA beat scGPT under the same setup (0.530). Image-only ResNet50 was weak (0.208), and multimodal fusion has not been tested at all. 2. Test: config_018 adds ResNet50 image features with concat fusion to the best RNA backbone, keeping profile setting, RNA encoder and aggregation fixed. Why now: Whether multimodality helps is the largest open design question and decides which part of the search space deserves the remaining budget. Anchoring it to the strongest known RNA setup gives a clean comparison against config_002. Evidence: the best result so far is config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA, ResNet50, avgpool, concat), with 0.619 accuracy and 0.610 F1. That is a modest gain over RNA-only avgpool (0.591), even though ResNet50 image-only is very weak (0.208). Avgpool has beaten the transformer for RNA, and PCA has beaten scGPT. The image encoder is still a completely untested design dimension, and the weak ResNet50 image features may be what limits the multimodal gain. Test: config_024 swaps only ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L and keeps every other setting from the best configuration. This isolates whether a stronger image representation improves fusion. Why now: it exploits the best-performing setup while removing uncertainty about a major representation choice. It is likely more informative than a fusion-type tweak (weighted vs. concat), whose effect is plausibly smaller. A clear gain would redirect the search toward ViT-L variants; no gain would suggest the image modality adds little regardless of encoder.

Evidence: the best results so far come from multimodal, multiprofile, PCA RNA with avgpool and concat fusion. ViT-L scored 0.629 accuracy and ResNet50 scored 0.619, a small gap. In the RNA-only runs, avgpool beat transformer aggregation (0.591 vs 0.519) and PCA beat scGPT (0.591 vs 0.530). The fusion strategy is still completely untested, since every multimodal run used concat. This experiment keeps the best configuration (config_024) fixed and changes only concat to weighted fusion, so any difference can be attributed to fusion alone. Weighted fusion may also help here because image features alone are weak (0.208 single-profile), and learned weighting could stop them from diluting the stronger RNA signal. This is the best use of the next experiment because it settles an untested design choice that applies across all multimodal configurations, while staying close to the current best region and so having a real chance of improving accuracy and F1.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_025 (PCA + ViT-L, multiprofile avgpool, weighted fusion; acc 0.635, F1 0.618). Two other findings support that setup. Avgpool beat the transformer for RNA-only multiprofile (0.591 vs 0.519). PCA beat scGPT under the same avgpool setup (0.591 vs 0.530). The largest untested factor is the RNA encoder scVI, which has not been tried in any configuration. Since RNA carries most of the signal (single-profile RNA 0.485 vs image 0.208), the RNA representation is probably a high-leverage choice. 2. What this tests: config_037 matches config_025 except that PCA is replaced by scVI (200 dimensions). This isolates the effect of the RNA encoder inside the strongest known multimodal setup. 3. Why this is the best use of the budget: It explores the one design dimension with no evidence yet. Because the rest of the setup is the best known, it also has a reasonable chance of beating the current best. If scVI underperforms, we can deprioritize the many remaining scVI configurations and focus on PCA-based variants, such as testing transformer aggregation in the multimodal setting.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_037 (scVI + ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1. That is about 7 points above the otherwise identical PCA version (config_025, 0.635). This RNA-encoder gain is the largest single-factor effect seen, but it rests on one comparison inside a multimodal model. scVI has never been tested in an RNA-only setting, and in unimodal multiprofile avgpool runs PCA (0.591) beat scGPT (0.530). 2) Test: config_005 is RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool with scVI. It changes only the encoder relative to config_002 (PCA) and config_008 (scGPT). It shows whether scVI is better on its own or only works well when fused with image features. It also measures how much the image branch adds on top of scVI. 3) Why now: The RNA encoder now looks like the most influential design choice. Confirming its effect cheaply, before spending budget on aggregation or fusion variants around config_037, will guide all later choices about scVI-based configurations.

1) Evidence: Within multiprofile RNA models, scVI with avgpool gives the best result so far (0.650 accuracy, 0.628 F1). Adding ResNet50 image features with concat fusion slightly lowered performance (0.632 accuracy, 0.607 F1). The single-profile ResNet50 image-only model is weak (0.208). The remaining open question is aggregation. Transformer was worse than avgpool in only one comparison (PCA RNA-only, 0.519 vs 0.591), so that is weak evidence that may not hold for stronger encoders or multimodal inputs. 2) Test: config_039 changes only the aggregation (avgpool to transformer) from the current best. 1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, avgpool, concat; accuracy 0.619, F1 0.610). It clearly beats the single-profile multimodal run, config_016 (0.527). If RNA-only multiprofile comes close to 0.62, image-side choices (ViT-L, fusion type) matter less and the RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT) should be prioritized.
